newsitem.title: RUSSIA: PM readies cabinet line-up, Yeltsin orders action.
newsitem.headline: PM readies cabinet line-up, Yeltsin orders action.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has prepared a long awaited new cabinet line-up and on Saturday laid the economic groundwork for Boris Yeltsin's Helsinki summit next week with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

The Kremlin says Yeltsin will announce the new team before flying to Finland on Wednesday. With ministers still in limbo, however, Yeltsin ordered the government on Saturday to sort out urgent funding crises in the army and the coal industry.

Miners have been prominent in planning a general strike on March 27. Some opposition politicians have also warned that low morale among the troops could leave Russia's rulers defenceless against the anger of a disillusioned populace.
"We are finishing our work on the structure (of the new government)," Chernomyrdin told ORT Television in an interview.
Some decisions would be unpopular but would be pushed through by a decisive, united team, he said. "We cannot drag out the process of reform, we cannot drag out people's suffering."

The whole structure of the administration would change under the guidance of liberal First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais. Some ministries covering industries which had now been largely privatised would be sharply cut back or scrapped.
Viktor Konnov, Chernomyrdin's spokesman, said the premier held three hours of talks with U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers at the government's White House headquarters.

The accent was on Russia's integration into world economic systems and admission into organisations like the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and Paris Club of government creditors.

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, who is expected to survive the cabinet reshuffle, left for Washington on Saturday seeking to prepare for a deal that could lead to a compromise on NATO's plans to expand, against Moscow's wishes, into eastern Europe.

The foreign ministry says Primakov has proposals to make. Primakov, who meets Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Saturday and Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday, also expects serious discussion on arms control.
Military problems of a rather different nature were exercising Yeltsin on Saturday, however.

Having accused his defence minister, Igor Rodionov, of "whingeing" recently over financial problems facing the armed forces, Yeltsin apparently heeded his warnings and issued an order to the government, saying simply: "Take steps urgently."
He was demanding action on short food supplies to the troops. But weekend newspapers had reports of wider problems.
The liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta said Rodionov gathered top commanders on Friday to discuss poor morale among officers.

General Alexander Lebed, ex-Kremlin security chief and one of Russia's most popular opposition politicians, said on Friday that the March 27 strike could be the catalyst for a social upheaval that would lead to the collapse of the administration.
Lebed said that, as in Albania, Russia's rulers could not count on the support of the army.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta said the possibility of an "Albanian scenario" was among issues considered in the Defence Ministry.

Yeltsin also gave the government two weeks to determine the coal industry's budget for 1997 and settle the state's debts to the sector run up in January and February. He emphasised that the social welfare of miners should have priority.
The miners, many of whom are among millions of workers unpaid for months, have played a prominent role in recent industrial action.
